entries.title: Brookfield Zoo welcomes newborn squirrel monkey
entries.summary: <p>Amid the humid mist and roaring waterfalls inside Brookfield Zoo’s Tropic World habitat, a new, tiny resident clung tightly to its mother and made an exclusive Sun-Times debut.</p><p>A newborn squirrel monkey born July 30 to mother Gizmo and father Sandy. While the infant does not have a name yet and its sex remains unidentified, it is already thriving, spending its first days riding securely on its mother’s chest and back as she navigates the habitat.</p><p>Guests will have a chance to see the newborn squirrel monkey and the rest of the primates inside the Tropic World exhibit daily during regular park hours.</p><p>The birth marks a milestone for the monkey troop and for Kim Skelton, director of primate care and conservation at Brookfield Zoo Chicago. Skelton brings 25 years of primate care experience from the Denver Zoo to the Brookfield team.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2018/10/31/18338371/2-baby-squirrel-monkeys-born-at-brookfield-zoo" target="_blank" >“Gizmo has had lots of babies</a> before,” said Skelton, but “this is Sandy, the father's, first infant. Skelton said that mother primates tend to serve as living models for their other offspring when it comes to motherhood. Allowing young females like Slim to observe daily interactions and practice key maternal behavior.</p><p>The troop of monkeys share their habitat with other animals, including capuchins, spider monkeys, and a giant anteater. The troop manages its own social structure smoothly, with Skelton noting that squirrel monkeys naturally stick to the mid-level branches while anteaters remain on the ground. The group also occasionally interacts with<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/metro-state/2025/02/18/brookfield-zoo-endangered-spider-monkeys-rescued-wildlife-trafficking" target="_blank" > neighboring spider monkeys</a>.</p><p>For now, the newborn will remain dependent on mom.</p><p>“That’s at least a few months before they start experimenting and getting off mom,” Skelton said. “It’ll be a while before they actually go off and explore on their own.”</p><p>As the infant grows, the primate care specialists will track key milestones, watching as the infant starts eating solid foods and engaging in social interactions without its mother nearby.</p><p>Another key milestone the Brookfield team will look for is when the infant starts using its long tail for balance. Unlike many South American primates with prehensile tails used for grasping, a squirrel monkey’s tail is longer than its body and functions more like a cat’s tail to help as they leap through trees.</p><p>“All of our births, whether it's a squirrel monkey, a gorilla, or a giraffe feed into our Species Survival Programs or captive management breeding programs that support not just populations within zoos, but potentially wild populations as well,” Skelton said.</p><p>That Species Survival Programs is managed through the Association of Zoos and Aquariums. These breeding initiatives maintain genetically diverse populations across accredited institutions, tracking lineages to safeguard species and support potential wild reintroductions.</p><p>“Every birth matters," Skelton said, "and we’re just pumped to have another little one popping around.”</p>

entries.title: Rubber duck race helps Special Olympics pay the bills
entries.summary: <p>More than 90,000 rubber ducks raced/floated/bobbed haphazardly toward the finish line near the Columbus Drive Bridge Thursday morning as thousands of spectators lined the Riverwalk to cheer them on.</p><p>It was all part of what has become an annual tradition to raise money for Special Olympics Illinois.</p><p>Since 2005, the Chicago Ducky Derby has invited people to adopt rubber ducks starting at $10 each, with bigger sponsor packs available. The ducks are dumped into the Chicago River and head toward the finish line. The money raised helps provide year-round sports programming, adaptive equipment and other resources for athletes with intellectual disabilities.</p><p>By noon, the riverfront near the Columbus Drive Bridge was packed with spectators holding up their phones, waiting for the dump truck to release more than 90,000 yellow rubber duckies into the water.</p><p>This year's event raised more than $700,000 for Special Olympics Illinois. The sponsor of the first-place duck won a new Chevrolet Trax. The second-place duck's sponsor won $2,500 in cash, and third place got four club seats to a Chicago Cubs game.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" entries.title: 57 decomposing bodies discovered at Far South Side funeral home
entries.summary: <p>Dozens of decomposing bodies were found Thursday at a Far South Side funeral home, according to the Cook County medical examiner's office.</p><p>A funeral was in progress when police, acting on a tip, showed up at South Chicago Chapel, 2939 E. 95th St., police said. Police had been told bodies at the home were not being stored at or below 40 degrees, as required by state regulations, according to a police report obtained by the Sun-Times.</p><p>Officers were met by funeral director Clark Morgan, who accompanied them on a walk-through of the building. During the walk-through, they found 57 bodies in various areas of the funeral home. The bodies were not refrigerated, and were in various states of decomposition, according to the police report.</p><p>At some point, officers left the building, and when they tried to go back inside. Morgan told officers that on the advice of his attorney, he wasn't letting them back in without a warrant. After officers told Morgan they did not need a warrant to inspect the building during operating hours, he padlocked the door and left, according to the report. Officers then called the Chicago Fire Department to help gain entry to the building.</p><p>The business’ license was revoked Wednesday, according to the police report.</p><p>The area around the home was blocked off by police Thursday night as some neighbors continued to mill about. </p><p>The foul smell that hung in the air Thursday night started during the winter, several neighbors told the Sun-Times.</p><p>One pair of neighbors were initially thrown off by the late hours people would be working at the funeral home. One, who worked night shift, said he’d often see in the lot past midnight.</p><p>They said they ended up putting up traps for the thousands of flies that emanated from the building. They, along with other neighbors, reported it to law enforcement six months ago, they said.</p><p>“We're grateful,” one neighbor said of the investigation. “I thought it was weird. … [But] we had an idea of what was going on.”</p><p>In a statement, the medical examiner’s office said it had been notified by Illinois and Chicago officials of the improperly stored bodies. Investigators and forensic pathologists went to the funeral home on Thursday and found "more than 50 decedents in various states of decomposition."</p><p>Staff from the medical examiner's office are "assessing the conditions of the remains, searching for documentation regarding identification of the decedents as well as death certificates. This process could take several days to ensure proper disposition," according to the statement. The office "will work with authorities to identify these decedents as quickly as possible and notify their families."</p><p>Another neighbor said whenever people would enter or exit the building for a funeral, “you could smell the rot.”</p><p>“We thought at first it was coming from a factory nearby, but it was like a rotting smell,” another neighbor said. “It smelled like an animal that was dead. … It wasn’t once or twice, it was every weekend. It was a fight to go outside and get in the car.”</p><p>“We just hope the families find their loved ones,” she added.</p><p>The Illinois Department of Financial and Professional Regulation suspended the license of the registered funeral director Johanna Morgan. Her husband previously held a a funeral director and embalmer intern license, which was revoked in 2024, according to the department.</p><p>That department alerted authorities after investigating.</p><p>A message left on the voicemail inbox of the funeral home Thursday was not returned.</p><p>A one-star Google review of the chapel posted two weeks ago complained: "HORRIBLE!! It smells and they are very unprofessional."</p><p><i>Contributing: Rosemary Sobol, Lauren FitzPatrick</i><br></p>

entries.title: Playoff expansion is No. 1 storyline ahead of the high school football season
entries.summary: <p>Is it time for a new catchphrase in prep football?</p><p>For decades, coaches have talked about the “drive for five,” which refers to the number of victories generally needed to clinch an IHSA playoff berth.</p><p>But this fall, that number will change for the first time in 25 years.</p><p>That’s the biggest storyline heading into the 2026 season. Here’s a rundown of a few to watch:</p><p><b>Expanded playoffs</b></p><p>For the first time since the IHSA went from six to eight classes in 2001, the postseason field is getting bigger.</p><p>After years of debate and various proposals, IHSA member schools voted to expand the playoffs by 50% from 256 to 384 teams.</p><p>That change has led to a few more, including the earliest start to football practice in state history on Wednesday. This year’s regular season starts on Aug. 20 in order to accommodate an extra playoff round and still finish the postseason over Thanksgiving weekend.</p><p>The new format introduces byes for the first time in the football playoffs’ 52-year history. Two-thirds of the teams will play in the opening round over the weekend of Oct. 23-24, with the winners advancing to the first round against bye teams Oct. 30-31.</p><p>Playoff guru Steve Soucie of Friday Night Drive has projected that all three-win teams will earn playoff berths along with two-win teams with a good strength of schedule.</p><p>The bar to reach the postseason has been lowered. But many coaches are still aiming for five wins or more in hopes of getting home-field advantage in the opening round or earning a bye.</p><p><b>Conference realignment</b></p><p>There are some new league alignments for 2026, though the pace of change has slowed from its peak.</p><p>After operating as a football-only superconference the last two years, the nine-team SouthWest Suburban and six-team DuPage Valley have gone their separate ways. Though the split has led to some scheduling challenges with nonconference games later in the season, it has allowed the restoration of rivalries that were paused during the merger.</p><p>The 24-team Catholic League is no longer co-branded with the East Suburban Catholic Conference, which disbanded at the end of the last school year.</p><p>There was shuffling throughout the league’s six divisions. Some of the highlights included Marist replacing St. Ignatius in the top-level Catholic Blue and defending Class 4A champion Montini moving to the Green to join reigning 5A champ St. Francis, 7A runner-up St. Rita and 6A semifinalist Nazareth.</p><p>The Public League also has a new look. In place of the former top-level Red Metro, which had 16 teams, are two top-tier, six-team divisions: the Red Star and Red Shield. What was formerly the top White tier is now the second-tier Red. The new White and the Blue round out the Public League tiers.</p><p><b>Holecek’s back</b></p><p>The biggest coaching change comes at Loyola, where John Holecek is back in charge after a three-year hiatus.</p><p>In his first stint from 2006 to 2022, Holecek turned a solidly successful program into arguably the state’s best. His teams went 185-36 with three state titles and four runner-up finishes.</p><p>He was succeeded by Beau Desherow, who led the Ramblers to state titles in 2023 and 2024. Loyola went 4-5 last season, its first losing record since 2002.</p><p>Holecek returned to the staff as an assistant and now begins his second act. Desherow has shifted to a newly created position of general manager of the football program as well as assistant head coach.<br></p>

entries.title: Sueños DJ, husband detained by immigration agents at Midway Airport despite pending asylum case
entries.summary: <p>Omar David Panqueva and his husband Santiago Paez had been set to depart on a flight to Washington D.C. to start a series of Karol G afterparties following her tour around the country Sunday.</p><p>Panqueva, known as DJ TUNJO, performed at Sueños Music Festival in Grant Park in May and the couple founded the Chicago-based Latin music and community event organization La Mesa Presents.</p><p>As they exited an Uber to go into Midway Airport, they were surrounded and detained by federal agents.</p><p>Silvia Paez, Santiago’s sister, described the two in social media posts as “not only partners, but a power team.” She said in a statement that the couple had been taken to a detention center in Indiana after being detained at Midway.</p><p>“They are good within the circumstances,” she wrote on social media. “[But] they are still separated.”</p><p>The Department of Homeland Security said it detained the couple for overstaying their 2021 visas that expired in 2022, but wouldn’t say if the two were accused of any crimes or had pending asylum cases the department was aware of.</p><p>Both will be held “pending removal hearings,” the federal agency said.</p><p>However, their attorney, Enrique Espinoza, said the two had pending asylum cases, and that those cases had been filed within the legally mandated time after their arrival in the United States, but the government was “skipping past that part.”</p><p>He said the couple had been cooperating with the government on the pending case, even providing the required biometric information.</p><p>“They have been proactive [in] requesting information about the status of their case, and the government said they were working on it,” Espinoza told the Sun-Times. “And here we are now with them detained even though they followed every rule by the government and have no criminal background. … It seems like they were just easy targets.”</p><p>A <a class="Link" href="https://www.gofundme.com/f/help-us-free-santiago-and-david-dj-tunjo" target="_blank" ><u>GoFundMe</u></a> for the couple’s legal defense and travel costs had raised $21,000 by Thursday evening. The couple’s lawyer didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.</p><p>Paez’s sister urged people to “be safe” and avoid airports. She also wrote that the support and “how much people are caring” was “one of the things keeping them strong.”</p><p>“Santiago and David are very aware of how the community has shown up for them,” Paez’s sister said. “They are so grateful for all of your support and your kindness, and overwhelmed by the love coming from you guys.”</p><p>In another social media, she said: "I wish we lived in a world where being Latino wasn’t a crime."</p>
